body.text: In the week when Prime Minister Anthony Albanese is meeting President Xi Jinping and other officials in China, let’s remember that people there are often more complex than they seem.

In September, maybe the speaker of Australia’s House of Representatives, Milton Dick, thought he was meeting just another Chinese foreign-affairs official during his visit to the country. Or maybe the speaker had been quietly told before the trip that there was much more to Yu Xubo than would appear on the gentleman’s business card.

The two met when the speaker and the parliamentary delegation he led were hosted in Beijing by the International Department of the Chinese Communist Party Central Committee on 20 September. Leading the Chinese team was the head of the CCP International Department, Liu Haixing. Also attending the meeting, at the right hand of Liu, was Yu, who Chinese media reports mentioned was a member of the Foreign Affairs Committee of the National People’s Congress (NPC), China’s rubber-stamp parliament. But Yu had other jobs, one of which would have been familiar to MI5.

As a parliamentary official, Yu was not a surprising inclusion in the itinerary of the speaker of the House of Representatives, one might say. However, rarely does Yu appear in the meetings hosted by the CCP International Department. And he has other identities that explain his attendance this time. Yu in fact serves as deputy head of the China–Australia Friendship Group of the NPC, and he had already met the Australian delegation in Guangzhou two days earlier. Yu then joined the later meeting between Milton Dick and Gao Xiang, president of the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences in his friendship-group capacity.

In addition to Yu’s parliamentary roles, he also serves as party head and president of one of China’s massive state-owned corporations, China General Technology Group, also known as Genertec. This state-owned enterprise is engaged in machinery-manufacturing, construction, real estate and pharmaceuticals. It operates domestically and internationally across Southeast Asia, South Asia, Africa, Eastern Europe and South America. Yu also serves on the BRICS Business Council and is involved in China–Canada parliamentary interactions.

Such a globally engaged cadre and company provide a very useful avenue for other functions of the Chinese party-state. Ten days after the Australian parliamentary delegation met with the CCP International Department officials, Britain’s counter-intelligence and security agency, MI5, issued a Security Service Espionage Alert:

MI5 has identified that the China General Technology Research Institute (CGTRI), sometimes translated as China Academy of General Technology (CAGT), has very strong ties to the Chinese Ministry of State Security (MSS), China’s civilian intelligence and security service. MI5 has identified that the primary purpose of CGTRI is to fund academic research that directly improves MSS technical capability for espionage.

The China General Technology Research Institute is a wholly owned subsidiary of Yu’s Genertec. The Institute’s links with the MSS will hardly be unknown to the president of the group. In fact, Alex Joske’s study Spies and Lies reveals that the China National Technical Import and Export Corporation, which is also a subsidiary of Genertec, is linked to the Shanghai State Security Bureau, which is under the MSS.

Yu has long links with Australia. Before 2020, when he was appointed to head Genertec, he was general manager and deputy party secretary of the China Oil and Foodstuffs Corporation, commonly known as COFCO. Yu was instrumental in COFCO Group’s 2011 acquisition of Australia’s Tully Sugar.

More recently, at the Boao Forum for Asia Annual Conference held in Hainan in March 2025, Yu Xubo was invited to participate in the China–Australia Business Leaders Dialogue – an event championed by Fortescue chairman Andrew Forrest – where he delivered a keynote speech on ‘Deepening China-Australia Cooperation and Promoting an Open Economy’. At the 2026 edition of the Boao Forum, Yu was again invited to address the China-Australia Business Leaders Dialogue, ‘sharing the group’s efforts to advance intelligent, green, and integrated development, and its path toward coordinated green growth and industrial upgrading.’

Some 13 years ago, John Garnaut, writing from Beijing, noted that some of Australia’s most high-flying business leaders had lately been feted in China by a ‘social organisation’ that had facilitated their access. They were unaware that the China Association for International Friendly Contacts was a platform for ‘influence operations’ by the Liaison Department of the General Political Department of the People’s Liberation Army.
So one does meet unusual people when visiting China. We hope that our security agencies are letting official Australian visitors to China know just how unusual their hosts may be.
ASPI’s China Defence Universities Tracker has also added a new Miscellaneous section, with a profile of CGTRI as its first entry.
